newsitem.title: UK: Britain vows full protection against IRA attacks.
newsitem.headline: Britain vows full protection against IRA attacks.

text.p: Britain vowed to protect Northern Ireland from growing guerrilla violence on Wednesday after police narrowly escaped a suspected ambush by IRA fighters overnight.
Sir John Wheeler, British minister for security affairs in Northern Ireland, sought to allay concern about a spate of incidents, saying extremists would be found and put behind bars.

Earlier, pro-British Protestant politicians demanded increased security after a bomb attack that looked like the latest stage in a campaign against British rule by the outlawed Irish Republican Army. No group claimed responsibility.
Police sources said officers had a lucky escape late on Tuesday when a device planted at by a road in Londonderry, the province's second city, exploded as their two armoured cars passed.
Wheeler said security was under constant review.

"There is nothing that the government can do to ensure that these terrorist crimes don't occur again, because they have been occurring in one form or another over the past 18 months, but what the police and security forces can do is to give the public the maximum possible protection," he told BBC radio.
"And they can guarantee this -- those who commit these crimes will find themselves being arrested, charged, going before the courts, being convicted and going to prison for a long time."
Wheeler urged pro-British Loyalist foes of the IRA to continue their 26-month ceasefire which he conceded was "very fragile".
Security sources suspect that the IRA carried out the Londonderry attack, probably using a home-made horizontally launched mortar bomb or a landmine.

The ambush, which was condemned by the main Irish Catholic nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party, came 36 hours after an IRA rocket attack injured a policeman in a security hut at the heavily protected law courts in Belfast.
That incident added to tension after a spate of recent attacks and bomb alerts, and it was followed by a series of bomb hoaxes that disrupted traffic in the provincial capital.

Politicians from the main pro-British Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) on Wednesday demanded an urgent meeting with police chiefs while a member of the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) said Britain must take on the guerrillas.
"The IRA are making it absolutely clear, for their part, that as far as they are concerned the war has started again," DUP spokesman Gregory Campbell said on BBC radio.

Campbell suggested that Britain should reinstate checkpoints and high-level security at the border with the Irish Republic where control on crossing points was eased during a 17 month IRA truce that ended in February 1996.

Five UUP members of the Northern Ireland Forum, an elected body boycotted by minority Irish Catholic nationalists, said they want to meet police chiefs to press for more patrols and other city-centre precautions to combat an IRA bombing threat.
